For example, in March 2021, the container ship Ever Green ran aground in the Suez Canal caused by a ship-wide power outage and sudden strong lateral winds, completely blocking the Suez Canal, as shown in Fig. 1. This incident resulted in a six-day disruption of the Suez route (Diaz and Neuman, 2021, CNBC, 2021).
For example, after the blockage of Suez Canal, the shipping company Rosatom strongly recommended that international trade can be conducted via the Arctic route

(Interfax, 2021). Meanwhile, Trutnev, the Russian Deputy Prime Minister, also expressed Russia's intention to turn the Arctic route into an alternative to Suez route in response to the disruption (Tickle, 2021). As another example, China Ocean Shipping Group has launched a sustainable Arctic shipping service since it crossed the Arctic in 2013 (COSCO Shipping, 2020), becoming an important alternative to the shipping of Suez route.
, the volume of navigation on the Arctic route has shown a year-on-year increase

. According to the data from Russia's Northern Route Administration, between 2016 and 2021, the annual cargo volume on the Arctic route increased from 7.43 million tons to 35 million tons, and is expected to exceed 110 million tons by 2030 (NSR Public Council, 2022). However, due to the cold climate of the polar Areas, the Arctic route is covered by sea ice for most of the year, requiring the assistance of icebreakers for smooth navigation. Meanwhile, the lack of infrastructure along the Arctic route and the difficulty of resupplying merchant ships have increased the cost of Arctic shipping. In addition, in June 2021, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted a resolution to “ban the use of heavy fuel oil (HFO) in Arctic shipping” (IMO, 2021). Inevitably, the ban for the use of HFO (i.e., the main shipping fuel) further increases the cost of Arctic shipping. Thus,
the Arctic shipping route is currently a potential alternative route rather than a mainstream route for international trade.

In addition to the shipping disruption risk, the carbon emission is another core factor affecting shipping. According to the Greenhouse Gas Study 2020 of IMO, more than 2 percent of annual global greenhouse gas emissions are emitted by shipping activities. If immediate measures are not taken, they will reach 3.5 times the level of 2012 in 2050 (Liu et al., 2022). For this reason, several countries and areas have introduced emission allowance policies. For example, in February 2023, the European Union (EU) passed a draft resolution to include the shipping industry in the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) by 2026 (Council of the EU, 2022). The trading system distributes emission allowance to companies and implements the policy of “selling more and compensating less”. In other words, companies can sell their unused emission allowance, whereas they have to buy the shortfall from other companies or pay a penalty (European Commission, 2023). It means that the impact of emission allowance will have to be taken into account in shipping activities.

Theoretically, although there is some literature discussing risk management problem (e.g., Wan et al., 2019, Qu et al., 2020, Zhao et al., 2023) and green shipping problem (e.g., Wang et al., 2015, Sheng et al., 2017, Liu et al., 2022) for shipping supply chains, but the literature considering both at the same time is not yet available. Specifically, there is a lack of research on the issue of shipping supply chain decisions when using the Arctic route as an alternative to the traditional route in the current context (i.e., growing shipping risk, emission allowance, and the European Union's ban on the use of HFO for Arctic shipping). Thus, this paper is dedicated to exploring this issue and shed light on the following research questions: (i) What is the optimal shipping strategy for the core company of supply chain with disruption risk? (ii) How do firms in the shipping supply chain make procurement and pricing decisions under disruption risk and emission allowance? (iii) How does the existence of shipping disruption risk/emission allowance affect the equilibrium decisions?

The contribution of this study is clear. Specifically, the work is the first to investigate the decision-making problem where Arctic route is used as an alternative option when traditional routes are disrupted. Arctic route is different from traditional route in terms of shipping distance, unit carbon emission, unit shipping cost, and emission policy. These factors cause a great deal of decision-making difficulties for companies. To deal with this problem, this study sets up a multistage decision model for shipping supply chain with disruption risk and emission allowance, and solves the equilibrium decision of each company in this supply chain. Thus, this work theoretically enriches the literature of shipping risk management, and the literature of Arctic route management. This work also provides decision-making solutions for supply chains when they face shipping disruption and emission allowance.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant literature. The model description is presented in Section 3. Section 4 provides analysis for the model. A case study is conduct in Section 5. The findings of the study are summarized and discussed in Section 6. All proofs are included in the Appendix.

There are three branches of previous research relevant to our study. The first branch is the risk management of shipping supply chain. Yang (2011) categorizes risks in the maritime supply chain into physical, operational, and financial risks based on the Container Security Initiative. Wan et al. (2019) design a model for assessing risk factors in shipping supply chain. It is found that dangerous goods transportation, fuel price fluctuation and competitive intensity are the higher risk factors. Qu et al. (2020) find that the number of initial orders for shipboard supply is determined by the reliability of highly flexible supplier and onboard consumption pattern. The cruise carrier can increase the wholesale price once this reliability is affected by natural disasters. Mańkowska et al. (2021) examine the impact of COVID-19 on shipping supply chain, and find that cargo volumes decrease but the transshipments increase on some ports at that time. Fan et al. (2022) use years of incident data from significant waters to develop a model that can be used for risk diagnosis and prediction. Zhao et al. (2023) argue that investment in accurate information benefits the port when upstream firms are optimistic to the market, but information sharing can threaten the carrier of information investment when the port is pessimistic to the market or channel competition is low. Jiang et al. (2023) study a new method for assessing risk in maritime supply chain and find that fuel price is the most important risk factor. In a nutshell, the risk factors and the corresponding impacts of shipping supply chain are identified by this branch of literature.

The second branch of literature focuses on the management of green shipping supply chain. McKinnon (2014) shows that about 40 % of shippers may control carbon emissions in the shipping supply chain, and only 6 % of shippers explicitly indicate that carbon reduction measures have been implemented. Wang et al. (2015) propose two trading options for reducing shipping carbon emissions, i.e., open-ended and maritime. Under the open-ended option, dry bulk carriers can purchase missing or sell excess emission allowances. Sheng et al. (2017) examine the impact of different emission regulations on the shipping supply chain. It is found that unilateral regulation may increase total emissions, while harmonized regulation is the opposite. Qiu et al. (2018) argue that ship sharing makes transportation firms to increase profits and reduce carbon emissions. Peng et al. (2021) develop an approach to optimize supply chain efficiency and reduce carbon emissions, which results the balance between benefit and environment. Liu et al. (2022) prove that information sharing is very beneficial to reduce wasteful carbon emissions, and it can achieve a win–win between ports and shipping firms with consumers' green preference. Zhou (2022) argues that total profits and carbon emissions of using low-sulfur oils are higher when both subsidies and consumers' low-carbon preference are low. The results are opposite when the two ranges are higher. Song et al. (2023) show that carbon tax may reduce the volume of containers at port, making ports and shipping firms. Huang et al. (2023) propose that shipping firms could improve the tripartite relationship and supply chain stability by sharing the cost of carbon reduction at ports. Overall, the ways to reduce emissions in shipping and its impacts on shipping supply chain were examined in the branch of literature. Different from these studies, this paper analyzes the impact of emission allowance on the decisions of shipping supply chain under disruption risk.

the Arctic route may be more cost-effective and energy-efficient than traditional shipping routes, making it a seasonal alternative to specialized shipping in the short term

. Zhang et al. (2019) argue that black carbon reduction is affected by Arctic shipping. Thus, all relevant parties need to integrate technology and operation, with attention on fuel adoption and operational transformation. Bennett et al. (2020) indicate the possibility that cross-polar route will be operational in the middle of the 21st century or even earlier. Joseph et al. (2021) analyze the loss cost, opportunity, and environmental risks of Arctic shipping based on a new systems model, which validates the economic viability of the Arctic route in different policies. trade. Christensen et al. (2022) find that the Arctic route from most of Northern Europe to East Asia is safe and saves distance, cost and carbon emission. Yercan and Sogut (2023) predict that as the climate warms, the Arctic route (including the Northwest channel) will operate year-round without icebreaker escorts. In brief, the branch of literature discussed the feasibility, economics, opportunities, and challenges of Arctic shipping. Unlike previous literature in the branch, this paper focuses on the supply-chain decision problems (such as production, purchasing, pricing, etc.) with Arctic shipping options.
